title: Make Fairness More Fair: Fair Item Utility Estimation and Exposure Re-Distribution

problem.claim: Item fairness in recommender systems concerns whether item exposure is consistent with item utility.

gap.claim: Most previous approaches estimate item utility from user-item interaction logs, commonly using click-through rate, but these observed-utility measurements may produce unfair item exposures.

contributions.claim: Argues that item utility should be modeled more carefully when assessing or allocating item exposure.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that observed-utility measurements may result in unfair item exposures.
The authors report that item exposure is uneven across items and that recommendation methods select the users who receive exposure.

narrative_sequence.summary: Item fairness has become a significant concern in recommender systems.
Fairness measurement depends on how item utility is modeled, with prior work relying mainly on interaction logs and CTR.
The authors argue that observed-utility measurements can lead to unfair exposures, in a setting where exposure is uneven and audience selection matters.

source_observation.claim: Fairness assessment depends on the item-utility model, and exposure is uneven across items.

interpretation.claim: Interaction-derived utility measures may encode or amplify exposure imbalance.

application.claim: When evaluating item fairness, examine how utility estimates and exposure allocation interact rather than relying only on observed CTR.

exception.claim: The supplied abstract units do not establish that CTR is always inappropriate or identify conditions under which observed utility is reliable.

unknowns: The proposed utility-estimation method is not described.
The exposure re-distribution mechanism is not described.
No datasets, baselines, metrics, or quantitative results are supplied.
The relationship between item utility and selected exposure audiences is not formally specified.
